theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Why is it best to handle short pastry with cool hands, and as little as possible?
options: So the pastry turns a darker colour when baked
So the water in the dough evaporates faster
So the pastry rises like bread in the oven
So the fat stays cold and the pastry is short

questions.stem: What does it mean when we say a pastry is "short"?
options: It has been rolled out very thin and long
It is crumbly and tender, not tough
It was baked for only a short time
It is cut into small, short strips

questions.stem: A basic short pastry uses half as much fat as flour. How much fat goes with 400 g of flour?
Plain short pastry is usually made by which method?
options: The creaming method
The whisking method
The rubbing-in method
The all-in-one method

questions.stem: Why is the water for short pastry added a little at a time?
options: Too much makes it sticky and tough
So the flour does not lose its colour
So the salt will dissolve more quickly
Because cold water freezes the fat

questions.stem: Why is short pastry rested in the fridge before it is rolled?
options: To let the raising agent start to work
So it relaxes, firms up and shrinks less
So the pastry can soak up more water
To make the fat melt evenly through it

questions.stem: How should you roll out pastry for a tart case?
options: Lightly and evenly, turning it a quarter often
Hard and fast, pressing down with your weight
With lots of flour, so it can't stick at all
Backwards and forwards in every direction at once

questions.stem: About how thick is short pastry usually rolled for small tarts, such as gizzada?
options: About 15 mm
About 10 mm
About 8 mm
About 3 mm

questions.stem: When lining a flan ring or tart tin, why do you lift the pastry in, rather than stretch it?
options: Stretching makes it sticky on the bottom
Lifting adds air to make the pastry rise
Stretched pastry shrinks back when baked
Stretching breaks the tin's non-stick coat

questions.stem: What does "baking blind" mean?
options: Baking with the oven light switched off
Baking pastry without checking it at all
Baking a pie with a lid and no holes
Baking a pastry case before it is filled

questions.stem: When baking blind, why is the case lined with baking paper and filled with baking beans?
options: To stop the base rising and the sides falling in
To add the flavour of the beans to the pastry base
To make the pastry cook more quickly
To keep the case soft for the filling

questions.stem: Why is a pastry base pricked with a fork (docked) before baking?
options: To make a neat pattern that the guests will like
To let steam out so it does not bubble up
To help the filling soak into the base
To check whether the pastry is cooked

questions.stem: A tart with a wet filling has a soggy, pale base. What is a likely cause?
options: It was not baked blind first
The pastry was rested in the fridge first
The oven was preheated to the right heat
The pastry was rolled evenly

questions.stem: Short pastry is tough and hard after baking. What is the most likely cause?
options: It was overworked or had too much water
It was rested in the fridge before rolling
It was rolled out lightly and evenly
The fat was cold when it was rubbed in

questions.stem: Short pastry is very crumbly and breaks when you try to roll it. What is the likely cause?
options: Too much water was added to the dough
It was rolled with a light, even pressure
The flour was sifted before mixing
Too little water was added to bind it

questions.stem: How is sweet pastry (pâte sucrée) different from plain short pastry?
options: It has sugar and egg, and is often creamed
It has yeast added so that it rises
It is made with vegetable oil instead of solid fat
It is folded many times like puff pastry

questions.stem: What is the filling of a Jamaican gizzada?
options: Spiced minced beef and onion
Sweet, spiced grated coconut
Ackee and saltfish
Mashed green banana and salt

questions.stem: The edge of a gizzada shell is often finished by hand. How?
options: Pinched all round into a frilled rim
Cut flat with a sharp knife, then brushed
Folded over the top to make a lid
Left rough and thick with no shape

questions.stem: How does puff pastry rise in the oven?
options: Yeast in the dough gives off gas as it bakes
Steam lifts the many layers of fat and dough
Baking powder mixed into the flour lifts it up
Air beaten into the eggs grows in the heat

questions.stem: Why is puff pastry chilled between each set of rolls and folds (turns)?
options: To let the yeast rest before the next turn
To firm the fat and relax the dough
To make the pastry easier to colour
To let the water drain out of the dough

questions.stem: In classic full puff pastry, how much fat is used compared with flour?
options: No fat at all
A quarter of the weight
Twice the weight
About the same weight

questions.stem: How should you cut puff pastry shapes so they rise evenly?
options: Twist the cutter as you press it down
Tear the pastry gently with your fingers
Press a sharp cutter straight down
Use a blunt knife and saw back and forth

questions.stem: Why is egg wash brushed only on top of puff pastry, not down the cut edges?
options: Egg wash on the edges makes them taste salty
The edges would turn too pale in the oven
It glues the layers and stops the rise
The edges would soak up too much of the egg

questions.stem: Puff pastry is baked in a hot oven. Which range is usual, as the recipe and oven maker say?
options: About 100–120 °C
About 200–220 °C
About 140–160 °C
About 280–300 °C

questions.stem: What usually gives the pastry of a Jamaican beef patty its yellow colour?
options: Turmeric or curry powder
Yellow yam mashed into it
Mango juice in the dough
Pumpkin cooked into the dough

questions.stem: The minced beef filling for patties must be cooked to what core temperature, or as the Centre's food safety plan says?
options: About 37 °C
About 50 °C
About 74 °C
About 100 °C

questions.stem: Why should a cooked meat filling be cooled before it is put into raw pastry?
options: Hot filling melts the fat in the pastry
Cold filling is easier to taste for salt
So the meat can be served raw in the middle
So the pastry can be rolled thicker

questions.stem: Baked beef patties are kept hot for sale in a warmer. At what temperature should they be held, or as the Centre's food safety plan says?
options: About 30 °C or above
About 45 °C or above
About 63 °C or above
About 20 °C or above

questions.stem: How is choux pastry different from other pastries?
options: It is rubbed in, like short pastry
It is folded in layers, like puff pastry
It is cooked in a pan before it is baked
It is made with yeast, like bread dough

questions.stem: When making choux paste, how is the flour added to the boiling water and butter?
options: A spoonful at a time over an hour
Sprinkled in slowly once the pan is cold
All at once, then beaten until smooth
Mixed with the eggs first, then added

questions.stem: What makes choux pastry puff up into a hollow shell in the oven?
options: Baking powder in the flour
Yeast added to the eggs
Layers of fat rolled in
Steam made in the paste

questions.stem: How do you know enough beaten egg has been added to choux paste?
options: It is stiff and will not move at all
It is as thin as milk and runs off the spoon
It has turned bright yellow all through
It is smooth and drops slowly from a spoon

questions.stem: Choux buns went flat soon after they came out of the oven. What is a likely cause?
options: They were baked until they were crisp and dry
They were taken out before they were dry
The oven was preheated before baking
The paste was piped onto a lined tray

questions.stem: Éclairs are filled with pastry cream (crème pâtissière). How should they be stored, or as the Centre's food safety plan says?
options: On a shelf in the warm kitchen all day
In the hot cupboard with the patties
Covered in the fridge at 5 °C or below
In a sealed tin at room temperature

questions.stem: How should freshly made pastry cream be cooled?
options: Left uncovered on the stove overnight
Put in the oven to keep it smooth
Mixed with cold water to cool it fast
Covered and chilled quickly

questions.stem: What is a pastry brush mainly used for?
options: Cleaning flour out of the mixer bowl
Brushing on egg wash, milk or glaze
Scrubbing burnt sugar off baking trays
Sweeping crumbs off the floor

questions.stem: Which tool cuts neat, even rounds of pastry for tartlets?
options: A rolling pin
A palette knife
A round cutter
A pastry brush

questions.stem: Some kitchens use a pastry sheeter, a machine with rollers. What is the main safety rule?
options: Keep the guards on and hands clear
Push the pastry through with your fingers
Run it with the guard lifted for speed
Clean the rollers while they are moving

questions.stem: Which allergens are in a plain short pastry made with flour, butter and water?
options: Eggs and fish
Nuts and sesame
Gluten and milk
Soya and celery

questions.stem: Some recipes use lard instead of butter in pastry. Why must this be shown on the label?
options: Because lard makes the pastry much sweeter
Because lard must be kept frozen at all times
Because the pastry will be more expensive
So guests who do not eat pork can choose

questions.stem: How should a block of unbaked pastry be stored for use the next day?
options: Uncovered on the shelf in the kitchen
Wrapped, labelled and kept in the fridge
In a bowl of cold water to keep it moist
Next to the oven so it stays soft

questions.stem: How are baked, unfilled tart cases best stored?
options: In an airtight tin until near service time
In the fridge, next to the raw meat and fish
Wrapped in a damp cloth so they stay soft
In the steamer, so they stay warm all day

questions.stem: Why are pastries for a buffet or display made the same size?
options: So the oven does not need to be cleaned
So the guests take more than one each
So the pastry needs less resting time
For a neat look, fair portions and cost control

questions.stem: What gives a shiny golden top to a baked meat pie or patty?
options: A dusting of flour before baking
A brush of egg wash before baking
A spray of water after baking
A layer of oil poured over after baking

questions.stem: After making pastry, how should the work surface be cleaned?
options: Wipe it with the same cloth used for raw meat
Leave the flour to dry and brush it later
Spray it with water and let it air dry
Scrape, wash, rinse and sanitise it

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to make short pastry by the rubbing-in method, and give the rules for keeping it short.
essays.modelAnswer: I weigh the ingredients: plain flour, a pinch of salt, and half the weight of the flour in cold fat, such as butter, margarine or shortening. I sift the flour and salt into a bowl and add the fat cut into small cubes. I rub the fat into the flour with my fingertips, lifting the mix up so it stays cool and takes in air, until it looks like fine breadcrumbs. I add cold water a little at a time and mix with a palette knife until it just comes together as a dough. I gather it gently, without kneading, wrap it, label it and rest it in the fridge. The rules are: keep everything cool, handle the pastry as little as possible, do not add too much water, and rest it before rolling, so it stays short and does not shrink.
markingPoints: Correct ingredients and ratio (half fat to flour), weighed
Rubs fat into flour with fingertips to fine breadcrumbs
Adds cold water a little at a time to bind
Handles gently, wraps and rests in the fridge
Rules: keep it cool, handle lightly, not too much water, rest before rolling

essays.stem: Describe how to line a tart tin with short pastry and bake it blind.
essays.modelAnswer: I lightly flour the table and the rolling pin and roll the rested pastry evenly, turning it often, until it is about 3 mm thick and a little larger than the tin. I roll it loosely around the rolling pin and lift it over the tin. I ease the pastry into the base and corners without stretching it, so it will not shrink, and press it gently against the sides. I trim the top edge with a knife or by rolling the pin over the rim. I prick the base with a fork so it does not bubble up. I rest it in the fridge again for a short time. I line the case with baking paper and fill it with baking beans. I bake it at the heat the recipe and oven maker say until the edges are set, then remove the paper and beans and bake again until the base is dry and lightly golden.
markingPoints: Rolls evenly to about 3 mm, a little larger than the tin
Lifts the pastry in without stretching and presses into the corners
Trims the edge and docks the base
Rests again, then lines with paper and baking beans
Bakes, removes the beans and bakes until the base is dry and golden

essays.stem: Describe how to make Jamaican gizzadas, from the pastry to the finished tarts.
essays.modelAnswer: I make a short pastry by rubbing cold fat into flour with a pinch of salt and binding it with cold water, then I rest it in the fridge. For the filling, I mix grated coconut with brown sugar, grated nutmeg, ginger, a little butter and vanilla, and cook it gently in a pan with a little water, stirring, until it is thick and sticky. I let it cool. I roll the pastry thinly, about 3 mm, and cut it into rounds with a cutter. I pinch the edge of each round all the way round to make the frilled rim that gives the gizzada its shape, and place them on a lined tray. I fill each shell with the coconut filling. I bake them at the heat the recipe and oven maker say until the pastry is crisp and golden. I cool them on a wire rack and label the allergens, such as wheat and milk.
markingPoints: Makes and rests a short pastry
Makes the spiced coconut filling and cools it
Rolls thinly and cuts even rounds
Pinches the rim and fills the shells
Bakes until crisp and golden, cools and labels the allergens

essays.stem: Explain how puff pastry is made and why it rises in layers.
essays.modelAnswer: Puff pastry is made from a dough of strong flour, salt and cold water, and a block of cold butter or pastry fat of about the same weight as the flour. The dough is rested, then rolled into a square and the fat is wrapped inside it. The parcel is rolled out into a long rectangle, always in one direction, and folded in three or in four. This is called a turn. The pastry is chilled in the fridge between turns so the fat stays firm and the dough relaxes. After several turns, there are hundreds of thin layers of dough and fat. In a hot oven, the water in the dough and fat turns to steam. The steam is trapped between the layers and pushes them apart, while the fat stops them sticking together, so the pastry rises into crisp, flaky layers.
markingPoints: Dough of strong flour, salt and cold water, with fat of about the same weight
Fat wrapped in the dough, then rolled and folded (turns)
Chilled between turns to keep the fat firm and relax the dough
Many thin layers of dough and fat are formed
In a hot oven, steam pushes the layers apart and the fat keeps them separate

essays.stem: Describe how to make and bake Jamaican beef patties safely, including the food safety points for the filling.
essays.modelAnswer: I make a flaky pastry coloured yellow with turmeric or curry powder, and rest it in the fridge. For the filling, I cook minced beef with onion, scallion, thyme, garlic, Scotch bonnet pepper and seasoning until it is cooked through to a core temperature of about 74 °C, or as the Centre's food safety plan says, checking with a clean probe thermometer. I add breadcrumbs to bind it, then cool it quickly, cover it and chill it until I need it. I roll the pastry, cut it into rounds, put cold filling on one half, wet the edge, fold it over and crimp it with a fork. I bake the patties at the heat the recipe and oven maker say until golden and crisp. They are served hot or kept in a warmer at about 63 °C or above. I keep raw meat apart from other food and wash my hands after handling it.
markingPoints: Makes a yellow flaky pastry and rests it
Cooks the filling to about 74 °C core, checked with a clean probe
Cools the filling quickly and keeps it chilled before use
Fills, seals and crimps the patties and bakes until golden
Hot-holds at about 63 °C or above and keeps raw meat apart

essays.stem: Describe how to make choux pastry and bake éclairs or profiteroles.
essays.modelAnswer: I put water, butter and a pinch of salt in a pan and heat it until the butter melts and the water boils. I take the pan off the heat and add all the sifted flour at once, then beat hard with a wooden spoon. I put it back on a low heat and beat until the paste is smooth and comes away from the sides of the pan in a ball. I let it cool a little. I beat in the eggs a little at a time until the paste is smooth and shiny and drops slowly from the spoon. I pipe it onto a lined tray as fingers for éclairs or small rounds for profiteroles. I bake in a hot oven, as the recipe and oven maker say, without opening the door at first, until they are well risen, golden and dry. I make a small hole to let steam out, cool them, then fill and finish.
markingPoints: Boils water, butter and salt; adds all the flour at once
Beats over heat until the paste leaves the sides of the pan
Cools slightly and beats in the egg gradually to the right consistency
Pipes even shapes onto a lined tray
Bakes hot without opening the door until dry; lets steam out, cools and fills

essays.stem: Describe three faults in pastry products, the likely cause of each, and how to prevent them.
essays.modelAnswer: Short pastry that shrinks in the tin was usually stretched when it was lined, or was not rested. I prevent it by lifting the pastry into the tin without stretching it and resting it in the fridge before baking. Pastry that is tough and hard has been handled too much or had too much water. I add water a little at a time and handle the dough lightly. A tart with a soggy base was not baked blind, the filling was too wet, or the oven was too cool. I bake the case blind and make sure the oven is properly preheated. Puff pastry that rises unevenly or leaks fat may have been rolled unevenly, cut with a blunt cutter, egg-washed down the edges, or become too warm. I roll evenly, cut straight down with a sharp cutter, egg-wash only the top and keep it chilled.
markingPoints: First fault with a correct cause
Correct prevention for the first fault
Second fault with a correct cause and prevention
Third fault with a correct cause and prevention
Uses correct terms (resting, baking blind, egg wash, turns)

essays.stem: Explain how to make, cool and store pastry cream (crème pâtissière) and other cream fillings safely.
essays.modelAnswer: To make pastry cream, I heat milk with vanilla. I whisk egg yolks with sugar and a little flour or cornflour, then whisk in the hot milk. I pour it back into the pan and stir all the time over a medium heat until it boils and thickens, and cook it for a minute or two so the flour is cooked. I pour it into a clean, shallow tray so it cools quickly, and cover it with film touching the surface so it does not form a skin. I chill it in the fridge at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says. I use clean piping bags and do not refill a used bag with fresh filling. Filled éclairs and tarts are kept covered in the fridge and used within the time the food safety plan allows. I label them with the date and the allergens: milk, eggs and wheat.
markingPoints: Makes pastry cream correctly and cooks it until thick
Cools it quickly in a shallow tray, covered on the surface
Chills at 5 °C or below, or as the food safety plan says
Uses clean piping bags and keeps filled pastries chilled
Labels with the date and allergens and uses within the allowed time

essays.stem: Explain the job of the flour, fat, water, salt and eggs in pastry.
essays.modelAnswer: Flour gives pastry its structure. Plain or soft flour is used for short pastry so it is tender, and strong flour, with more protein and gluten, is used for puff and choux so the layers and shells are strong enough to hold their shape. Fat makes the pastry short by coating the flour so the gluten does not develop too much. In puff pastry, the fat keeps the layers apart. Butter gives the best flavour and colour, while shortening or lard gives a very short pastry. Water binds the dough together, and in puff and choux it makes the steam that lifts the pastry. It must be cold for short and puff pastry. Salt gives flavour and strengthens the dough. Eggs enrich sweet pastry and bind it, and in choux they hold the air and set the shell. Egg wash gives a golden shine.
markingPoints: Flour gives structure; plain for short pastry, strong for puff and choux
Fat makes it short and keeps the puff layers apart
Water binds and makes steam for lift; kept cold
Salt gives flavour and strength
Eggs enrich and bind; in choux they help it rise and set

essays.stem: Explain how to finish, present and store a tray of mixed pastries for a hotel buffet.
essays.modelAnswer: I plan the tray so it has a good mix, for example gizzadas, fruit tarts, éclairs and small beef patties. Every piece is the same size so the tray looks neat, the portions are fair and the cost is controlled. I finish each item just before service: glazing fruit tarts, dusting with icing sugar, or dipping éclairs. I arrange them in neat rows on clean trays or stands, with sweet and savoury items apart, and I handle them with tongs or gloves, not bare hands. Each item has a label with its name and allergens, such as nuts, wheat, milk and eggs. Cream-filled pastries stay in the fridge until service and are kept on a chilled display at 5 °C or below. Patties are kept hot at about 63 °C or above. Both are used within the time the Centre's food safety plan allows.
markingPoints: Plans a varied tray with same-sized pieces for neatness and cost control
Finishes items close to service
Arranges neatly and handles with tongs or gloves
Labels each item with its name and allergens
Keeps cream items chilled and patties hot, within the plan's time limits

practical1.title: Make short pastry by hand and produce gizzadas and baked-blind tart cases
practical1.brief: Work in the Centre's training kitchen, in clean uniform with hair covered. As a group, read the recipes, list the allergens and set up the work area. Each member makes their own batch of short pastry by the rubbing-in method, by hand, and rests it in the fridge. The group cooks one pot of spiced coconut filling for the gizzadas, with each member doing a named stage (weighing, grating or measuring the coconut, cooking and stirring, cooling). Then each member rolls their pastry to about 3 mm, cuts and pinches 6 gizzada shells, fills and bakes them, and lines and bakes blind one small tart case. The group fills the tart cases with pastry cream or a fruit filling the assessor gives, finishes them neatly, labels everything with name, date and allergens, and cleans down. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Plain flour, salt, cold butter, margarine or shortening, and cold water
Grated or desiccated coconut, brown sugar, nutmeg, ginger, butter and vanilla for the filling
A filling for the tart cases (pastry cream or fruit), as the assessor gives
Scales, bowls, palette knives, rolling pins, round cutters, small tart tins and tartlet trays
Baking paper, baking beans, a pan, wooden spoons and a wire rack
Oven, dry oven gloves, cling film, labels and pens, and cleaning materials
photos: The group in clean uniform with the work area set up and allergens listed
Fat rubbed into flour to fine breadcrumbs
The pastry wrapped and labelled for resting in the fridge
Pastry rolled evenly and rounds cut
Gizzada shells pinched and filled on the tray
A tart case lined with paper and baking beans
Baked gizzadas and finished tarts cooling or on display
Products labelled with name, date and allergens, and the clean work area
checklist: Washed hands, wore clean uniform with hair covered and no jewellery
Weighed the ingredients accurately with the right fat-to-flour ratio
Rubbed in lightly to fine breadcrumbs and added the water a little at a time
Rested the pastry, then rolled it evenly to about 3 mm
Shaped and pinched gizzada shells neatly and filled them evenly
Lined a tart case without stretching it and baked it blind correctly
Baked the products until crisp and golden at the correct heat
Labelled with name, date and allergens and cleaned the area and equipment
safety: Use dry oven gloves and tell others when you are carrying hot trays
Take care with the hot sugar filling: stir with a long spoon, keep hands clear of splashes and let it cool before filling
Keep knives and cutters on the board, not near the edge, and wash them straight after use
Wipe up flour and spills at once so nobody slips
Keep the pastry cream chilled at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says

practical2.title: Make rough puff pastry for beef patties and choux pastry for éclairs
practical2.brief: Work in the Centre's training kitchen, in clean uniform with hair covered. As a group, read the recipes, list the allergens and set up. The group makes one batch of yellow rough puff pastry (with turmeric or curry powder) for patties, with each member doing at least one roll-and-fold turn and the pastry chilled between turns. While it rests, the group cooks the beef filling; one member checks and records the core temperature (about 74 °C, or as the Centre's food safety plan says) with a clean probe thermometer while the assessor watches, and the filling is cooled quickly. Each member makes their own small batch of choux paste, pipes 6 éclairs or profiteroles and bakes them. Then each member rolls, fills, seals and crimps at least 3 patties, egg-washes them and bakes them. The group fills the cooled choux with chilled cream or pastry cream, finishes them, labels everything with name, date and allergens, and cleans down. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the temperature record to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Strong and plain flour, salt, cold butter or pastry fat, turmeric or curry powder and cold water
Minced beef, onion, scallion, thyme, garlic, Scotch bonnet pepper, seasoning and breadcrumbs
Water, butter, eggs and flour for the choux, and cream or pastry cream for filling
Rolling pins, palette knives, round cutters, forks, piping bags and nozzles, and a pastry brush
Lined baking trays, a pan, a clean probe thermometer and a temperature record sheet
Oven, dry oven gloves, labels and pens, and cleaning materials, with colour-coded boards if the Centre uses them
photos: The group in clean uniform with the work area set up and allergens listed
Rough puff pastry being rolled and folded, showing the layers
The probe thermometer in the beef filling, with the reading recorded
Choux paste dropping slowly from the spoon, and shapes piped on the tray
Patties filled, sealed and crimped before baking
Baked patties and choux, risen and golden
Filled and finished éclairs or profiteroles
Products labelled with name, date and allergens, and the clean work area
checklist: Washed hands, wore clean uniform with hair covered and no jewellery
Did a roll-and-fold turn correctly, keeping the pastry cold
Kept raw meat apart and washed hands after handling it
Took part in cooking the filling to the safe core temperature and cooling it quickly
Made choux paste to the right consistency and piped even shapes
Filled, sealed and crimped patties neatly and egg-washed only the tops
Baked all products correctly without opening the oven early for the choux
Kept fillings chilled, labelled the products and cleaned the area and equipment
safety: Use a clean probe thermometer and sanitise it before and after each use
Use separate boards and tools for raw meat, and wash hands after handling it
Take care with the hot choux pan and boiling water: use a long spoon and keep the handle turned in
Use dry oven gloves for hot trays and wipe up spills at once
Keep cream fillings chilled at 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says
